newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus partners in crucial meeting Friday.
newsitem.headline: Airbus partners in crucial meeting Friday.

text.p: Partners in Europe's Airbus consortium will meet on Friday to try to hammer out agreement on restructuring to allow it to compete better with archrival Boeing.
A spokesman for Airbus partner British Aerospace Plc said he was sure the restructuring would be discussed but he could not say whether substantive accords would come out of the meeting.
A spokeswoman for France's Aerospatiale said she did not know what would be on the agenda, while an official in the press office of Airbus in Toulouse referred queries to partner firms.

The meeting takes place against a background of a changed civil aircraft market after Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said last month they would merge and form a civil and military behemoth with nearly $50 billion in annual sales.
The deal surprised the aircraft-making world and prompted calls for Airbus to speed up its planned transition from a partnership to a leaner, more flexible corporation.
The partners said on July 8 they aimed to reach an agreement by the end of 1996 on a timetable for setting up a new Airbus company which could be formed by 1999.
But the partners remain deeply divided over how to structure a new company, senior industry executives have said.
France's Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale wants a "minimal" Airbus which would act as prime contractor with enlarged powers to direct subcontractors.

But Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG seeks to deepen Airbus integration to include design and engineering of sub-assemblies as well as making the major systems such as wings and fuselages. This "maximum Airbus" would also handle procurement, final assembly and product support.

British Aerospace, which is a 20 percent partner, wants to transfer core assets, including design and manufacturing facilities, from the partners to a new company and provide it with a strong balance sheet to finance aircraft sales, executives have said.
The Airbus spokesman said another crucial issue likely to be discussed was a plan for a large aircraft to compete with Boeing's 747 jumbo jet.
The 747 is the only commercial jet capable of carrying more than 400 passengers and Airbus would dearly like to challenge Boeing's lone grip on a profitable segment of the market.
Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain, which holds four percent of Airbus, is the fourth partner.
